title: Bed at 6:45am - US Open semi-finalists fight effects of late-night finishes
description: New York is known as the city that never sleeps. But that comes at a price for US Open stars - including men's semi-finalists Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev.
fullText:
New York is known as the city that never sleeps - and so it has been at this year's US Open.

A number of matches have started late and finished in the early hours, backing up the city's reputation as a playground for the nocturnal.

But when some players - including men's semi-finalists Ben Shelton and Alexander Zverev - are heading to bed as Manhattan commuters are waking up for work, it raises questions about fairness.

Three of top seed Zverev's five matches over the past fortnight have finished past 1am.

"I've been to bed as late as 6:45am in the past week so I'm kind of a bit jet-lagged," Zverev said.

"I feel like I'm playing the Australian Open in New York right now."

Friday's semi-final against Karen Khachanov - not before 15:00 local time/20:00 BST - will be the first time the German has played in the day at this year's US Open.

American eighth seed Shelton did not complete his last-eight victory over Carlos Alcaraz until 3:34am on Wednesday.

Shelton faces 11th seed Frances Tiafoe, who wrapped up his quarter-final about 19:00 on Tuesday after beating US compatriot Alex Michelsen in a five-set epic.

"The advantage of the opponent who has played earlier in the day will be big - they've had that full evening's rest and a good night's sleep," Matt Little, who was Andy Murray's long-time strength and conditioning coach, told BBC Sport.

"We can all relate to it - if you have one really bad night's sleep, you have the knock-on effect of that for the coming days."

Little saw the effects first hand when Murray infamously finished a match at 4am at the 2023 Australian Open, with the former world number one managing only three hours sleep before returning to Melbourne Park about 11am the following day.

Zverev did not go to bed until gone 5am following his opening three victories at Flushing Meadows and stayed up to watch Shelton beat Alcaraz on his night off.

Shelton, who meets Tiafoe in Friday's night session (19:00 local time/00:00 BST, Sat), insisted he would pull up "all right" after two days off court.

"He'll have to be napping to catch up some sleep," said Little.

"On the nutritional side, he'll be making sure he gets as many carbs and as much protein as he can in for that next match, and trying to get back to a bit of a routine.

"It's about making sure you can optimise the hydration and get as much sleep as possible without completely going into a full slumber."

Murray described the situation in Melbourne - where he beat Thanasi Kokkinakis in the second-latest finish in Grand Slam history - as a "farce".

Few disagreed, and slight tweaks have been made in an attempt to limit matches finishing at the crack of dawn.

In response to Murray's match, the Australian Open cut the number of day-session matches on the main courts from three to two to reduce the risk of night sessions being delayed.

In early 2024, the ATP and WTA created new rules which prevented tour matches - played over three sets and not five like the Slams - starting after 23:00. These rules, however, do not apply at the majors.

Last week, former world number one Venus Williams and her opponent Sofia Kenin began their first-round match at 12:13am - the latest start in US Open history.

It was one of three matches which finished post-2am in the first seven nights, with three others ending after 1am, while Shelton's victory over Alcaraz was the latest finish in US Open history.

"Something has got to give," said 18-time Grand Slam singles champion Martina Navratilova. "This is not OK and it is not normal."

Some argue these occasions are the essence of the US Open - and a raucous sporting representation of the city which never sleeps.

The volume of early-morning matches has increased at Flushing Meadows this fortnight, although Tuesday's play finishing at 3:34am on Wednesday was the product of unusual circumstances.

All three preceding quarter-finals on Arthur Ashe Stadium - Aryna Sabalenka beating Linda Noskova and Jessica Pegula overcoming Emma Navarro, with Tiafoe's win sandwiched in the middle - went the full distance.

Data shows matches are becoming longer - so what is the solution?

Starting the US Open night sessions earlier is the most common proposal.

That is met by a resistance from television executives and the practicality of New York life, with many fans unlikely to arrive at Flushing Meadows much before 7pm.

There is a more extreme suggestion - cutting back on the best-of-five sets format at the Slams.

That idea gained further traction after Andrew Abdo - Tennis Australia's recently-appointed chief executive - suggested the Australian Open could look to reduce men's matches to three sets in the future.

Abdo's comments provoked a backlash, with Tiafoe among those defending the traditional way.

"Do I love five-setters? Absolutely not," Tiafoe said.

"But it's tennis, man. I grew up watching so many incredible five-setters.

"Novak-Rafa, Federer-Rafa, epic five-setters that go on for hours and hours. That's the history of the game."

fullText:
PlayStation 5; Insomniac Games
Logan is well realised by Liam McIntyre and some exquisite character art, but there are lapses in narrative and emotional arcs and some of the combat feels like a chore

It was always going to be difficult to follow Spider-Man. Insomniac’s three games based around the web-slinger are masterpieces of superhero wish fulfilment, allowing you to swoop above a depiction of Manhattan alive with graffiti artists, roving journalists and gun-toting gangsters. If anyone should be up to the task, it’s Wolverine. A beloved Marvel stalwart, his life much darker and bloodier than Peter Parker’s, he seems the ideal protagonist for a moody action adventure. Yet somehow this well-made game falls short of its potential.

Set years before the founding of the X-Men, Marvel’s Wolverine sees a disenfranchised Logan falling back in with Sabretooth and Mystique when their mentor Nathaniel Essex is kidnapped by mutant-hating billionaire Bolivar Trask. This archetypal tech bro has a disturbing plan for world domination and the X Team are out to stop him – but there is a secret buried in Wolverine’s past that’s about to cause an eruption. It’s a decent setup, filled with the sort of intrigue, violence and Freudian tension we expect from the X-Men.

At its heart, though, Marvel’s Wolverine is, like its hero, an unreconstructed brawler. From the start, you can dodge, parry, shred attack and leap attack with speed and savagery, but as you earn XP, you unlock new techniques and combos as well as powerful special moves such as the tornado spin, which damages enemies all around you in a flurry of blades, or the spiral strike, which lets you drill through an enemy to escape a crowd. Your main combo attack is the barrage, accessed by hitting shred repeatedly, but this can be closed with a leap attack or other unlocked techniques for extra damage, and to stagger opponents. On top of this you can also unlock new DNA strands, which provide buffs to your health and cooldown speeds. The highlight, though, is the three-stage rage meter, which builds as you damage and parry enemies. At each stage you get more powerful attack and defensive stats, and at the final stage you become an almost indestructible machine of carnage, which is immensely liberating.

But while fights feel smooth and empowering, there is rarely any need to be creative or experimental. In the Spider-Man games, the character’s grace, his web-throwing, the three-dimensional nature of his movement, all encourage you to fight beautifully; here I was reminded of 80s beat-’em-ups, or PS3 brawlers – a bludgeoning production line of identical fights against increasingly over-familiar enemy types. Sure, this fits with Wolverine’s character, but similar melee-based brawling adventures such as Devil May Cry and Bayonetta provide deeply layered combat systems and diverse enemy types which reward (and often demand) varied techniques from players. I survived a huge majority of skirmishes in the default difficulty setting by pummelling parry and switching between linked shred attacks and leaps, opening and closing barrage combos in the process, while letting rip with specials whenever they came online. The boss battles, which felt extremely familiar and at times cliched, demanded a similar approach, just with better timing and more patience.

Similarly, the Insomniac team warned us to expect a more tightly structured environment than in the Spider-Man titles, and they were not kidding. Wolverine is mostly linear, thrusting us from set-piece to set-piece in a globe-trotting race against time and plausibility. When we do get to big, inviting cities such as Madripoor or Tokyo, we find roads closed off and invisible walls directing us back to the action. The whole world feels like a theatrical backdrop, untouchable and aloof, and many miles from the bustling metropolis we got to live in and explore as Spidey. Yes, we all know this makes sense – Wolverine is by nature a rootless character, an inveterate drifter, but presenting us with a Tokyo so richly detailed and visually seductive, only to lock most of it off, feels almost cruel.

In contrast, the game’s interpretation of Logan is a triumph. Through exquisite character art and animation, and a brilliant performance from Liam McIntyre, he comes alive as a flawed, often unwilling hero, capable of extreme brutality and touching vulnerability. His rivalry with Sabretooth and his blossoming relationship with Jean Grey are intricate and involving, resulting in some truly moving scenes. But you play no interactive part in the linear story or its relationships, and the few attempts at offering puzzles tied in with the narrative are hurriedly designed and quickly abandoned. We’re told that Wolverine’s past trauma will be explored, but for much of the game this comes via snippets of lore that you unlock by competing in mini-challenges such as timed parkour runs and horde battles against waves of baddies. It feels like a rather insensitive way to portray and process PTSD. The climax of the game, when it comes, is an absolute technical marvel, a Homerian clash of super powers, but sadly its impact is lessened by far too many exposition flashbacks and airy metaphysical deviations.

Marvel’s Wolverine remains a lovingly crafted, beautifully polished hack-’em-up that will no doubt thrill Wolverine fans who want to eviscerate as many enemies as possible while looking out for X-Men easter eggs, and pausing once in a while to have story and subtext thrown at them. But despite the full-bloodied use of Wolverine’s claws and a generous array of moves and combos, combat lacks both the bone-crunching impact of the Batman Arkham games and the balletic joy of Spider-Man. As the game goes on and the enemies line up, it feels increasingly like a chore. Logan becomes what he always dreaded: hired muscle.

There is so much seductive and emancipating rage in this game, in its story, its combat mechanics, its gloriously conflicted protagonist. But the crescendo always feels like it’s just out of reach, like an argument in another room, or a war on the news.

title: Titans scouting report vs New York Jets: Matchups, edges, our score prediction
description: With the New York Jets coming to town to start Robert Saleh's tenure as Tennessee Titans coach, it's easy to get caught up in the past. Let's serve the present.
fullText:
The only thing that no one's going to talk about as the Tennessee Titans prepare for their season opener against the New York Jets is the game itself.

The Titans host the Jets to start the 2026 NFL season at Nissan Stadium on Sept. 13 (noon CT, CBS). All the scuttlebutt about Titans coach Robert Saleh's past life coaching the Jets and the fleet of former Jets he signed to rebuild the Titans roster and the smaller fleet of former Titans who've ended up playing for the Jets and the broad, general misery that these two fanbases have endured in the last few seasons figures to overshadow the game itself which, by all accounts, should be one of the week's least compelling.

The Jets and Titans come into the year tied for the third-worst odds to win the Super Bowl per BetMGM. Jets QB Geno Smith feels like an obvious stopgap. Titans QB Cam Ward has massive expectations he needs to start living up to. Jets coach Aaron Glenn might already be on the hot seat. And Saleh's got to prove his poor results with the Jets weren't because of bad philosophy, but because of a bad situation.

Still, there's plenty of talent on both sides of the ball, and more than a few matchups worth watching.

The Jets' secondary famously didn't intercept a pass in 2025, so more than a little bit of work went into revamping it. In one offseason, the Jets added veteran Nahshon Wright, Minkah Fitzpatrick and Dane Belton and second-round pick D'Angelo Ponds. Combine those additions with edge defenders David Onyemata and David Bailey, the No. 2 pick in the draft, and the Jets have a new arsenal of weapons to prevent passing success.

So, obviously, do the Titans in the inverse. Ward adds Wan'Dale Robinson as a go-to slot option and third-down specialist and No. 4 draft pick Carnell Tate as his deep threat, intermediate target and red zone favorite. Throw in Calvin Ridley's return from injury and there's a good argument that Ward will be throwing to three receivers who are all more talented than what his best options were at the end of last season.

This matchup of revamped weakness turned potential strengths might be the story of the game. Whoever more successfully installs their new toys takes a huge advantage.

KEEP READING: For his next trick, Brian Daboll aims at Cam Ward and improving Titans | Exclusive

The Jets have early-round pedigree just about everywhere on offense. Receiver Garrett Wilson and running back Breece Hall are studs. Tackles Olu Fashanu and Armand Membou are developing nicely. Rookies Kenyon Sadiq and Omar Cooper Jr., are extra toys to use on the perimeter. There's a lot of talent here, even if there are questions about Smith's viability as a starting-caliber quarterback.

That ability to attack the Titans on the outside might be an advantage, especially with the criticisms defensive backs like Alontae Taylor, Cor'Dale Flott, Amani Hooker and Kevin Winston Jr., drew throughout training camp. But the Titans also have the advantage up the middle, with defensive linemen Jeffery Simmons and John Franklin-Myers representing a best-case scenario for how to attack an offense through the A and B gaps.

Saleh's defense is about attack mentality and going full speed instead of reacting to keys. If Simmons and Franklin-Myers are successful enough getting off the ball that the Jets can't get the ball to the perimeter, consider the Jets' strengths neutralized. If not, well, the Titans begin at a disadvantage.

The uncomfortable reality is that the Jets might be the more talented team overall. But they're in a messier spot than even the Titans, and the Titans' greatest strengths are a little more developed and easier to deploy. Saleh's defense carries the way in this one.

Nick Suss is the Titans beat writer for The Tennessean. Contact Nick at nsuss@gannett.com. Follow Nick on X @nicksuss.

title: Tennessee Titans vs. New York Jets: 3 key matchups for Week 1
description: The Titans' week one matchup against the Jets features three key matchups, including Cam Ward vs. their revamped secondary and more.
fullText:
The Tennessee Titans' Week 1 matchup against the New York Jets could come down to a handful of individual battles when the two teams meet at noon CST this Sunday.

Both teams enter the opener looking to establish a new identity. Tennessee is beginning its first season under head coach Robert Saleh, who previously coached the Jets, while New York is entering Year 2 of the Aaron Glenn era after going 3-14 last season (same as the Titans).

The Titans are slightly favored at home, while the projected total of 39.5 points suggests a defensive battle. With that in mind, here are three key matchups that could decide the Titans' Week 1 matchup against the Jets.

The most obvious matchup starts with Tennessee's second-year quarterback. Cam Ward's performance against the Jets' revamped secondary could determine just how successful the Titans' offense is in its first game under offensive coordinator Brian Daboll.

Ward enters his second NFL season with the benefit of a much deeper group of offensive weapons around him, including newcomers WR Wan'Dale Robinson and rookie WR Carnell Tate. However, the Jets have made changes in their secondary to improve a unit that struggled mightily last season.

New York added veteran safety Minkah Fitzpatrick, among others, to create more stability on the back end after not recording an interception throughout all of 2025. If Ward consistently finds Tennessee's playmakers and forces the Jets' secondary to defend the entire field, the Titans could have an opportunity to control the game. However, if New York can confuse Ward, the matchup could quickly swing in the Jets' favor.

The Titans' biggest advantage could come in the trenches, with Jeffery Simmons playing his first game under Robert Saleh's system. Tennessee has also surrounded him with several players who fit the defensive identity Saleh wants to establish, including former Jets defensive linemen Jermaine Johnson and John Franklin-Myers.

If Tennessee can generate interior pressure without constantly blitzing against Jets QB Geno Smith, Saleh can devote additional resources to defending Garrett Wilson and the rest of New York's receiving corps. Simmons' ability to collapse the pocket and disrupt the run game will be key to forcing Smith to throw when he doesn't want to.

Another battle of the trenches headlines this Week 1 matchup of teams hoping to reverse their recent struggles. The Jets used their second overall pick of the 2026 NFL Draft to select edge rusher David Bailey, who expects to get plenty of playing time despite appearing on their depth chart as a backup.

Former Titans nose tackle T'Vondre Sweat will also man the middle under the direction of defensive-minded head coach Aaron Glenn. The Titans have some changes along their offensive line group that allowed 56 sacks (6th most in the NFL) in 2025.

Protecting Cam Ward is key to his success against the Jets' secondary, and this will be the Titans' first true test of improvement since last season.

title: Tesla crashes into scaffolding in Midtown Manhattan, killing passenger
description: Two 27-year-old females were in the vehicle when it crashed.
fullText:
A Tesla crashed into scaffolding in Midtown Manhattan on Wednesday morning, killing the vehicle's passenger and sending the driver to the hospital, according to police.

A preliminary police investigation revealed that a gray 2024 Tesla Model Y SUV driven by a 27-year-old female collided with scaffolding, a bus stop and a mailbox at approximately 2:43 a.m. on Wednesday, a New York Police Department spokesperson told ABC News.

The driver was traveling eastbound on East 42nd Street and failed to navigate the roadway, police said.

Emergency medical services responded on the scene and transported the driver and a 27-year-old female passenger to the hospital, where the passenger was pronounced dead and the driver is in stable condition, according to police.

title: A NYC firehouse was first to respond on 9/11. 25 years on, Sal Argano is the last still on staff
description: Sal Argano got lucky.  When the World Trade Center was struck by hijacked jets on Sept. 11, 2001, the New York City firefighter was in Brooklyn, on loan to another station, rather than at his usual po...
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — Sal Argano got lucky. When the World Trade Center was struck by hijacked jets on Sept. 11, 2001, the New York City firefighter was in Brooklyn, on loan to another station, rather than at his usual post at the small Manhattan firehouse just across an intersection from the twin towers.

He rushed downtown to find his firehouse badly damaged but still standing. Six of its members, he'd later learn, were among the 343 New York City firefighters killed in the World Trade Center's collapse.

"If I wasn't sent out on rotation there would have been a good chance I would not be here today," Argano says. "I think about that all the time."

Almost 25 years later, Argano, now 65, is still on duty at the firehouse — the last of the firefighters assigned there in 2001 who still works there.

Today, the crews at the firehouse respond to emergency calls but also serve as a de facto part of the 9/11 memorial, visited by crowds of tourists daily.

Some visitors come specifically to see the large bronze relief along the side of the building listing the names of the firefighters killed on 9/11.

Others pause to take selfies as they pass by on their way to the National 9/11 Memorial plaza across the street, drawn by the sight of Engine 10 and Ladder 10, the gleaming trucks sitting in the garage that give the station its nickname: Ten House.

"This is definitely one of those companies where if you don't want to ingratiate yourself to the public, it's definitely not the right place," said Capt. Terence Brody, who commands Ladder 10 and has worked at the station since 2016. "People around the world know this firehouse. They're going to come by and say hello."

Brody, now 55, was still in the fire academy on 9/11. Cadets grabbed their gear and were bused to ground zero.

The debris hung so thickly in the air around the fallen towers that it looked like it was snowing, he said.

"It was a beautiful sunny Tuesday, and then you're in this kind of apocalyptic atmosphere," Brody said. "It was a little overwhelming, to say the least."

In the days after the attack, Ten House served as both command center and safe space for weary first responders, he said. As the years passed, its crew had a front-row seat to the area's rebirth.

Robert Favata joined Ladder 10 in 2008, fresh out of the academy.

In those early years, he worked beside a giant hole teeming with construction activity. Now 46, he looks out at a transformed landscape.

A pair of waterfall pools sit in the footprint of the old towers, ringed by parapets etched with the names of nearly 3,000 victims. Below ground, the 9/11 Museum houses mangled steel beams, a destroyed fire truck and other artifacts. New skyscrapers ring the memorial.

"When I got here, there was nothing," Favata says. "I never thought they were gonna finish."

Argano can be found most days perched near the station's open bay doors, patiently answering questions, shaking hands and posing for photos.

He says Ten House firefighters have a unique charge: they're both living testimonials to the events of 9/11 as well as public faces of the centuries-old FDNY.

Argano says he tries to impress on younger firefighters — many increasingly not even born before the attacks — the importance of treating every visitor with respect.

"This is not like any other firehouse," he said. "We have our fire duty, we have our responses, and then we have a responsibility toward the people outside."

He acknowledges the task is not always easy. The packs of gawking tourists can be relentless. Their questions can sometimes come across too personal, too insincere or just simply too out there.

Many of the younger firefighters tend to keep a lower profile for that reason, he said.

After responding to an early morning call this particular day, most of the crew heads to the back of the station to stow their gear or upstairs to help prepare lunch.

Argano meanwhile chats up a firefighter from France and his wife and then invites them into the station.

He points to a wall of patches from fire departments across the world that have been gifted over the years, as well as the well-worn helmets hanging in the rafters.

At another point, though, a lady asks — perhaps a bit too flippantly — what's so special about Ten House.

Argano shrugs: "It's just a fire station." After she departs, he says it simply wasn't worth the effort.

"If I need to explain to you all of that, then it's like, 'Pull up a seat'," Argano said. "Let me get another cigarette. It's gonna be a long one."

Favata considers the approaching 25th anniversary as likely one of his last before retirement. He worries, though, if he's done enough to keep the memories of Ten House alive.

"When I got here, so many of the guys worked 9/11 and they told me their stories of that day," Favata said, choking on tears. "I just hope I can give like a percentage of what they've told me to the younger guys."

Brody, meanwhile, handed in his retirement papers Tuesday. His last day will be in October.

"It's interesting to think that my first day in the field was right across the street, and this is where I'm gonna end my career," said Brody, who writes screenplays in his spare time and has already had two of them turned into Hallmark Channel movies.

But Argano, who drives Engine 10, isn't quite ready to pack it in. He fears something will be lost when no one is there who still remembers.

"I'm not done. I'm gonna be here as long as I can," Argano said. "I'm going to keep telling them what I know, what I saw, what I've been through. Telling them the history of this firehouse. Everything I can remember."

description:

Plus: Americans think they have it bad with unwanted surveillance. They should visit London

Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you after visiting Coney Island in New York City, where I ate a hotdog, rode a ferris wheel and enjoyed a quintessentially American summer holiday.

Today in tech, we’re examining OpenAI’s new model release and the Silicon Valley’s monopoly power, and wondering why Brits and Americans have such vastly different opinions about surveillance cameras.

OpenAI released a new artificial intelligence model this week, Astra, just as more concerning reports are emerging about hacking by a rogue agent in July.

OpenAI’s president, Greg Brockman, heralded the new model as “artificial general intelligence” (AGI), a fuzzy term that at its basic level means an AI that is more capable than a human being at intellectual tasks. “It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” he said.

But if the announcement sparked amazement, it was as much cause of concern.

In July, OpenAI revealed that its AI agent, a type of software capable of carrying out tasks autonomous in response to human instruction, had gone rogue during safety testing and hacked a developer forum, Hugging Face. Last week, news broke that the agent had not only hacked Hugging Face, but also a German website, and that different AI agents had staged conversations with each other and seemed to have discussed how to collaborate on breaking containment.

OpenAi had delayed Astra’s release due to concerns over its cybersecurity capabilities, even announcing a supposed pause on developing its AI in the middle of August. That pause seems to have been short-lived, only two weeks.

The combination of Astra’s capabilities and OpenAI’s recent disclosures points to a worrying future. If the model is better at hacking than its predecessors and smarter than a human, will the future consist of one cyber-attack after another, forever, launched autonomously and without oversight, by rogue AIs? (Please not.)

OpenAI itself has warned of this future. The startup’s chief global affairs officer told a Guardian reporter in late August that people should prepare to defend against “ongoing, persistent” cyber-attacks.

As ever, though, we should take fever-pitched warnings about AI with a grain of salt that tastes like marketing. It is great business to be the creator of near-omnipotent technology, especially if you need to gin up excitement – fearful or positive – that will hype up your upcoming debut on the stock market.

Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal

New York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high school

Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’

Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI

Child sexual abuse survivor alleges Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used photos of her to generate new illegal images

The US is in the throes of a major political backlash against technology. We’ve talked in this newsletter before about the hatred of the hyperscale datacenters, which power artificial intelligence and have blanketed the US. And now there’s a secondary wave of contempt sweeping the nation.

Cameras – automated license plate readers, to be specific – made by Flock Safety are inspiring ire and violence across the country. These cameras snap pictures of car’s license plates as they drive by. According to Flock, about 120,000 cameras erected across the US conduct 2bn scans of license plates per month.

Like datacenters, the cameras offer a physical object to resist, unlike a social network or a piece of software. It’s quite a lot easier to protest a gigantic ugly building or an ominous black camera on the side of the road than it is to give up Instagram.

Widespread video surveillance in the US isn’t entirely new. In the aftermath of the terror attacks of 11 September 2001, the US government vastly increased the scope of its surveillance of telephonic and digital communications. Flock now offers local law enforcement a nationwide searchable database of license plate scans, and police officers have been documented abusing it egregiously to stalk their romantic partners.

In the UK an estimated 1m surveillance cameras are operational, and they have not drawn a similar level of political heat.

London erected the “ring of steel” surveillance cordon, which included the wide deployment of CCTV cameras, in the early 1990s, in response to bombings by the Provisional Irish Republican Army.

Both countries went through their surveillance evolutions roughly a decade apart. Those 10 years saw rapid advances in technology that defined the public spaces that governments wanted watched – physical town squares or the digital one – and growing awareness of the profound impact of tech surveillance on the general public. Simply put, the UK went through its transformation at a time when surveillance by tech companies was not top of mind. And Americans aren’t accustomed to cameras on every corner the way Londoners are. We’re more likely to joke that each of us has a personal FBI agent monitoring our search history.

In addition, there hasn’t been an era-defining violent incident on the scale of 9/11 or the IRA bombings that would have softened the American public to cameras watching their cars. So instead, Americans are destroying them for fun.

fullText:
Exclusive: Documents show officers from Maine to California worry Meta’s camera-equipped glasses will be used either to secretly record them or aid acts of terrorism

In January, the New York police department’s counter-terrorism unit sent out a memo warning police officers about a new potential “security and counterintelligence” threat: Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

The memo directed officers to “conduct thorough inspections of all eyewear permitted within inmate cells” and cautioned that people who have been arrested could use these glasses, equipped with small cameras and microphones, to record inside police facilities. The memo cited two examples of such videos posted on social media.

“The ability to covertly record inside a law enforcement or detention facility, could result in a security risk if proprietary information about cell layouts, camera placements, or officer patrol/site protection routines are released,” the memo read.

The NYPD memo is one of a dozen, previously unreported and reviewed by the Guardian, that showed law enforcement agencies across the US are increasingly concerned about the potential for smart glasses to be used against them. Officers from Maine to California worry the technology will be used either to secretly record officers and facilities or to aid in the execution of crimes and acts of terrorism.

One of the videos, taken with smart glasses and posted to TikTok in July 2025, offered a rare peek into a South Carolina detention center that had been the subject of a federal investigation over unsafe conditions.

“Everyone here is trying to figure out what’s going on with my glasses, why my light is blinking,” the user said about other detainees in the video. “People don’t know about Meta glasses.” He filmed a dingy shower, the inside of holding cells, an overcrowded cafeteria, and several other detainees as they slept, ate or walked, all seemingly unaware of being recorded.

Detention facilities in the US typically confiscate any and all devices that would be capable of recording video footage. Some Meta smart glasses have gone unnoticed, though. The glasses are discreet and can pass as a regular pair of Ray-Bans or Oakleys. Their main differentiator is a small blinking light in the corner of the frame that is activated when the glasses are recording.

The covertly recorded videos prompted the NYPD’s intelligence and counter-terrorism bureau, a specialized unit that works with the FBI to monitor and prevent terrorist threats, to send out the January memo to other police departments. The glasses “may appear as ordinary prescription eyewear”, the memo read.

US police and federal agents are not alone in their fear. Concern among the public and privacy experts over Meta’s smart glasses, widely dubbed “pervert glasses”, is growing. The technology enables its wearers to record people without their consent and has already been used to harass people.

Documents obtained by Property of the People, a non-profit that works to increase government transparency, show law enforcement agencies have grown as equally worried as everyday people about being filmed without their knowledge.

Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of Property of the People, said the documents show that law enforcement officials want the exclusive right to use surveillance technology and cameras to monitor the public without those cameras being turned back on them.

“These agencies surveil the public incessantly, but the moment we can watch them back, it’s deemed a security threat,” Shapiro said. “When only the government is allowed to hold the camera, that’s not security. It’s impunity.”

“The potential for smart glasses to be used by residents and the general public to conduct surveillance and other nefarious activities has introduced additional risks and concerns in Department of Corrections and law enforcement facilities,” read a memo distributed in June 2026 by Maine’s fusion center. Fusion centers are Department of Homeland Security facilities spread across the country as surveillance hubs that collect and analyze what the DHS describes as “threat-related” information from local law enforcement, private companies and other state and federal agencies.

“Some smart glasses can leverage AI software including facial recognition, which could lead to doxing of publicly available information or connections to law enforcement officers,” the Maine document continued.

Other memos expressing concerns about Meta smart glasses originated from the DHS’s joint counter-terrorism assessment team and fusion centers nationwide, including in San Diego, California, Tennessee, Virginia, Maine and New York.

Those fears have been enough to prompt federal agencies to bar their own employees from using the smart glasses in the workplace. In August, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency said that smart glasses qualify as body-worn cameras, which means they can’t be worn in the “federal workspace”, according to a memo the New York Times obtained. The “use of Meta Glasses or similar devices could unintentionally capture, record or transmit sensitive information”, the memo, written by ICE’s acting director David Venturella, read.

Meta says its glasses “are designed to be noticed”.

“Every pair has a bright white LED that blinks when a photo or video is taken for your gallery, it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or tampers with the LED, the camera is disabled,” said a Meta spokesperson, Dina El-Kassaby.

Beyond being filmed without their consent, law enforcement agencies are also cautioning that these glasses may be used to aid in planning or “reconnaissance” for violent acts of terrorism or “hostile pre-operational surveillance”. A January 2025 NYPD memo cited the New Year’s Day terror attack in New Orleans, when a man rammed his truck into a crowd on Bourbon Street, killing 14 and wounding 35 people.

The FBI had alerted local agencies like the NYPD that the perpetrator of the attack biked around Bourbon street twice at the end of 2024 wearing smart glasses. The FBI alleges the perpetrator conducted “pre-attack target reconnaissance”. Officers should be aware of and report individuals “acting in a suspicious manner observed wearing what may be smart glasses”, the memo states.

Evan Greer, the executive director of digital advocacy non-profit Fight for the Future, said they were not surprised police are concerned about the technology being used against them or to cause harm.

“Surveillance makes all of us less safe,” Greer said. “There’s no such thing as Meta glasses that are only for the good guys.”

The French quarter is a highly trafficked tourist area, Meta spokesperson El-Kassaby said, arguing that the perpetrator could have filmed the French Quarter with any other recording device including a phone.

The concern over Meta’s smart glasses is part of a broader concern expressed by law enforcement officials over the ways the proliferation of artificial intelligence-backed technology may impinge on police activity, the documents show. Law enforcement are at once looking for ways to use AI for investigative purposes and warning against public opposition to its use.

In an August 2025 document, the NYPD wrote that while new AI technology could “significantly transform day-to-day police operations” that police would also need to address public fears about the use of advanced tech in policing.

The memo was a response to “AI 2027”, a paper written by a former OpenAI researcher and other industry experts proffering what the future of AI development could look like and the effect it will have on society. It warns that AI opposition could result in “anti-tech violent extremist activity” and civil unrest over job losses, the widespread use of deepfake technology, and loss of trust in government and tech.

Anti-tech violent extremist activity isn’t a formal DHS designation for categories of terrorism but has recently cropped up in law enforcement messaging about a broad spectrum of extremist opposition to AI. Experts worry it could serve to criminalize all anti-tech opposition and the constitutionally protected right to protest.

title: NYC releases trove of 9/11 documents showing officials knew air quality at Ground Zero was unsafe
description: The release of more than 170,000 pages of records comes days before the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.
fullText:
New York City on Tuesday released more than 170,000 pages of records showing that officials knew the air quality around Ground Zero following the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks was unsafe despite repeatedly assuring residents and first responders the air was safe to breathe.

The documents — including previously unreleased air quality reports, contamination records and memos between officials — were posted online by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office days ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks.

"On Friday, we will mark 25 years since the worst tragedy to ever befall our city, the darkest day New York City has ever known," Mamdani said at a news conference surrounded by 9/11 survivors and families. "And yet, the devastating truth is that the suffering did not end once the smoke cleared and the dust settled. For so many New Yorkers who lived or worked or studied near Ground Zero, and for the thousands of others who worked on the pile, recovering those we lost and clearing the rubble, that was only the beginning."

Nearly 3,000 people were killed in the attacks. But according to Mamdani, more people have died from 9/11-related illnesses than were killed on the day itself.

"People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air," Mamdani said.

The mayor was joined by Jon Stewart, host of The Daily Show and a longtime advocate for first responders and people with 9/11-related illnesses.

"There was poison in the air, and on the ground, and in the windowsills, and in your air conditioners and covering your pets and your clothes, and it stayed there for months," Stewart said. "Everyone knew. Now it's very clear that the city knew as well."

The records, which had been stored in 68 boxes in a city office, were discovered last year, according to the mayor's office, and posted to a searchable online database. They include the so-called Harding memo, sent to then-Mayor Rudy Giuliani's deputy mayor, Robert Harding, in which officials discussed ways to limit the city's liability for toxic exposure.

Their release follows the settlement of a pair of lawsuits brought by 9/11 Health Watch, which had sued to force their publication. More documents are expected to be posted to the portal in the coming months.

"The very least our city owes the families, survivors and first responders whose lives were forever changed by the September 11th attacks is transparency and accountability," Mamdani said in a statement. "For too long, New Yorkers have had to fight for access to records that should have been available to them in the first place."

Mamdani is scheduled to attend more than a half-dozen events this week marking the 25th anniversary of 9/11.

In an appearance on Newsmax over the weekend, Giuliani said Mamdani's decision to attend them "offends" him, repeating baseless and Islamophobic claims about the city's first Muslim mayor and comparing him with the 9/11 terrorists.

Mamdani declined to respond directly when asked about Giuliani's comments on Monday.

"I'm proud to be the mayor of this city. I love this city. I love this country," Mamdani said. "And what I want this week to be a focus on is the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of Sept. 11, and a focus also on the first responders who did everything they could for this city."

fullText:
Erika Kirk, the wife of the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, in a new New York Times opinion piece published Monday discussed the words she recounted receiving from second lady Usha Vance after her husband's death.

In her essay, Erika Kirk says that the day after her husband was fatally shot, she had a conversation with Vance.

"I don't know how I'm going to do this," Kirk says of her conversation with Vance, to which the second lady replied, "You know when you're on an airplane with your kids, and you're going to land in 15 minutes, but the kids are going crazy, screaming, throwing things, and then the plane lands, and the kids relax, and everything is fine again?"

"That's how it will be. Just get through the next 15 minutes," Vance told Kirk, according to her Times piece.

Kirk wrote that Vance's "words are seared into my heart."

"Grief is strange. Time continues even when every part of you wants it to pause or, better yet, rewind. But the people we love who have passed on would not want us to spend the rest of our lives trying to rewind. At first, I needed to survive the next 15 minutes. Over time, I've realized that Charlie would want me to live them," she added.

Charlie Kirk was fatally shot on Sept. 10, 2025, while giving a speech at Utah Valley University.

During a memorial service honoring her husband in late September last year, Erika Kirk broke down at one point as she said she forgave the suspect who allegedly shot and killed him. Kirk spoke at length about her husband's mission and the centrality of religion in her family during the event.

"I love you Charlie, baby. And I will make you proud," Kirk said when ending her speech, to which the audience responded with strong applause.

Last month, Turning Point USA announced that Charlie Kirk will be honored at an event Thursday on the Utah Valley University campus, near where he was shot.
